verdictOnCurrentFilms: Honest read: these are slideshows with subtitles, and nothing in them is acted. Three things are wrong in all three films. (1) Every film is the same machine: a picture centred over a blurred, colour-sampled copy of itself, one rounded translucent caption pill in a Georgia-style serif, a tiny credit line top right. Ford, Douglass and Persia are indistinguishable except for the pictures, so none matches its exhibit (no Anton, no Abril Fatface, no Cormorant, no signal red, gold or lapis anywhere). (2) Motion has no intention: in each contact sheet two of six frames, nine seconds apart, are the same image at the same size and the same caption position, so the image sat dead for 9 to 18 seconds; the only motion we can see is a dim-to-black dip (Douglass frame 3 is a half-faded engraving with a ghosted caption, which reads as a glitch, not a transition). Nothing arrives, settles or leaves; there is no anticipation, no overlap, no held-then-released beat that matches a narrator breath. (3) Layout collisions: on Persia the caption pill sits on top of the seal photograph, and on Douglass and Ford the caption crowds the bottom edge of the image; the blurred fill puts a muddy mustard wash behind the 1845 title page and a grey smear behind Ford's portrait, which tints evidence by proxy even though the photograph itself is ungraded. What is right and must survive: the archive plates are real, uncropped and sit large; Reconstruction is labelled in the credit line (but at 8 px it is a footnote, not a label); the Quadricycle street, the stele court and the empty press-style frames are the strongest paintings. Reconstructions of a faced Ford at the lamp are fine only because he is turned away. The fix is not more effects; it is giving each film a body: a way things enter, a weight, and a hand.
concept: The Hand That Sets the Page. Each film is one object being physically handled by the exhibit's own craft, and every title, caption, plate and transition is that craft's gesture, performed with weight. Ford: a stencil and a punch, a plate slammed down on a bench. Douglass: type being composed, locked up, inked and pulled. Persia: a scroll or road-map being unrolled along one line of travel. Partition: a line being drawn on a map, in madder red, and the plates tearing along it. The shared grammar across the family (so they read as siblings): (a) the archive plate never animates its pixels, only its mount does: it arrives on a mount, with a 4 to 6 frame settle (anticipation, overshoot 2 percent, settle) and then holds absolutely still except a barely-there 1.5 percent drift that never touches the image tone; (b) every animated thing has an arc and a settle, no linear moves, and a one-frame hold on impact that the eye reads as weight; (c) text is physically set, never faded in word by word (the council struck word-by-word reveal) so each text arrives as a whole, in one gesture; (d) RECONSTRUCTION is the only tracked caps and it gets its own physical stamp, so it shouts. Motion is the acting; the narrator is the script; the design councils own the surface.
titleSequence: About 7 seconds, 24 fps, skippable in the player. 0.0 to 0.5 s: black, then room tone. One real archive plate (never graded) is placed by the exhibit's gesture on a dark ground in the exhibit's own colour (iron, iron-gall, midnight, soot), on its true-edge mount with the credit under it. 0.5 to 2.4 s: the exhibit's own title object builds. Ford: ANTON caps in #ff4b1f, 'HENRY FORD' stencilled in two beats, the stencil mask lifts off with a 2-frame jitter; a stamped serial plate reads 'DETROIT / 1863-1947'. Douglass: ABRIL FATFACE title assembled from three slab lines that drop into a composing stick one line per beat with a 6-frame squash on impact and gold #d9b36a ink bleed settling in 8 frames; 'FREDERICK DOUGLASS' as the locked forme. Persia: CORMORANT GARAMOND title in lapis #4f7cff, with large real Syriac (Noto Sans Syriac) and Chinese (Noto Serif SC) at 6 percent faded behind, drifting 12 px over the whole title as a slow road. Partition: FRAUNCES title in Urdu, Hindi, Punjabi, English one over the other, a single madder #e8553d line draws across between them over 18 frames (ease-in-out, slight tremor) and each title hangs on the line. 2.4 to 5.5 s: hold, the narrator's first breath is already audible under it; subtitle (dates) arrives on the beat of the first score note. 5.5 to 7.0 s: the title object exits with the gesture reversed in 70 percent of its entry time (exits are quicker than entrances), the plate stays and the film begins on it. The Enter-equivalent: no gate, nothing to wait for; narration starts under the last second of the title.
typography: One face per exhibit, one shared system voice. Ford: Anton for titles and year stamps at 140 to 220 px, caps, tight; Plex Mono or Courier Prime for the typed index tag. Douglass: Abril Fatface at 120 to 180 px for titles with wood-type slab (Clarendon/Playbill-class, e.g. Alfa Slab One) only for single-word broadside stamps; caption body Source Serif 4. Persia: Cormorant Garamond 90 to 140 px, regular weight, wide leading, real Syriac and Chinese as a faded layer, readable at full size when they are the subject (the stele and the Syriac book), never decoration. Partition: Fraunces at 110 to 170 px with real Noto Nastaliq Urdu, Noto Sans Devanagari and Noto Sans Gurmukhi at equal weight to the English, native-reader proofed. Shared system voice: Source Serif 4 captions at 40 px on 1080p (readable on a TV), Inter Tight 400 for credits at 24 px minimum (not 8 px), RECONSTRUCTION in Inter Tight caps +12 percent tracking in the exhibit's hot colour inside a stamped box, the only tracked caps in the family. Per-exhibit treatment: Ford type is stencil-masked and lands with a punch; Douglass type is letterpress-inked, 3 percent ink squash and a faint deboss on the plate; Persia type is rubbing-ink, soft edge; Partition type is cut along the map line. Never gold foil gradients, glow, or letterspaced tiny caps.
captionsAndLowerThirds: Kill the rounded translucent pill. Captions are set as plain text with a hard black 80 percent band only when over a plate, 0.8 s ease-out, bottom-safe at 9 percent from the edge, never overlapping the plate (the plate sits in the top 68 percent, the caption owns the bottom 24 percent; this removes the Persia seal collision). Caption lines arrive as a whole block on the narrator's first stressed syllable and leave 6 frames after the last word; they do not typewriter or fade word by word. Narrator breaths are visible as a one-frame gap between caption blocks. Key words (a year, a place, a number) are set in the exhibit's hot colour with the same weight, no bold, no size jump. Lower third (names, places, dates) is a single line with a 2 px rule in the hot colour that draws left to right in 10 frames, text sits on the rule, holds for the length of the name plus 1.5 s, and retracts in 6 frames. The credit becomes a real line at 24 px below the plate: institution, year, licence. RECONSTRUCTION is a stamped box that slaps onto the corner of any generated painting at the first frame, with a 3-frame squash and a held 6-frame rest, and stays until the cut; below it, one line of 28 px naming what is evidence and what is imagined.
transitions: 1. THE PUNCH-IN (Ford, plate to plate): the outgoing plate is pushed off its bench by the incoming plate sliding in from the right, 14 frames, ease-out cubic, 3 percent overshoot and a 3-frame settle, a one-frame frame-line flash in #ff4b1f on contact; used between factory-era plates, on a narration beat. 2. THE LOCK-UP (Douglass, section change): four black slab bars slide in from the edges like a forme being locked up (8 frames), a single ink-pull wipe in iron-gall brown (10 frames, 4 percent texture), then the bars retract on the new plate; used at section changes only, about 4 per film. 3. THE PAGE LIFT (Douglass, within a section): the plate lifts 12 px with a 6-frame fade of its mount shadow, a 2-frame dip to the ground, and the next plate drops with a 4-frame squash; used when the narrator pauses. 4. THE ROAD UNROLL (Persia): a single horizontal line travels across at one eased speed (24 frames, accelerates then glides), carrying a strip of the next plate behind it like a scroll opening; used for every place change; the same line later becomes the Silk Road in the infographic. 5. THE TORN LINE (Partition): a thin madder line draws top to bottom (18 frames) and both plates split along it, each half shifting 12 px opposite directions then settling with a 4-frame rebound; used only at the Radcliffe-line beat and at one other, so it keeps its force. 6. THE HOLD (all films): a hard cut on a narrator's consonant with a 12-frame hold, no effect, used when a document is the subject (the Narrative title page, the Radcliffe map, the Independent masthead); the plainest cut is the strongest here. 7. THE BEAT-CUT (all films, music-led): hard cut on a score downbeat, no more than twice per film, to a plate that has been half-seen as a thumbnail in the corner for 12 frames, so the cut is anticipated. 8. THE DIP TO MOUNT (all films, end of film): the plate dims to its own scan-edge frame over 18 frames and the narrator's last line sits above a single credit roll; no black dip anywhere in the middle of the film.
motionGraphics: Ford: (a) a stamped parts-bin tag animates on 'ninety-three minutes' versus 'twelve and a half hours': two Anton numerals counting down from 750 minutes to 93 in 40 frames with an easing curve that decelerates sharply into the last 12 digits, then a punch stamp. (b) A stencil chassis outline draws along a horizontal assembly rail under the 1913 plate, 7 stations, each labelled in Plex Mono, travelling at line speed; the line stops at the station the narrator names. Douglass: (c) a composing-stick title card where the year '1845' is set, lifted, inked and pulled onto paper over 36 frames with an ink-squash settle; (d) the Narrative title page held for 5 s with the narrator's words, and 'Written by Himself' traced by a thin gold underline that draws once, in 14 frames; (e) wood-type single-word stamps (FREE, BOSTON) as 1-second broadside inserts, never over a face. Persia: (f) one map of the road drawn as a single lapis line from Antioch via Seleucia-Ctesiphon to Chang'an, travelling at a drawn pace with a small stop at each named city and the Syriac name unfolding beside the Latin; the camera follows the line head, not the whole map. (g) Large real Syriac and Chinese script on the stele plate: the narrator reads the line and the script lights from right to left (Syriac) or top to bottom (Chinese) in the reading order, 1 line per second; the credit to the translator comes up with it. Partition: (h) the Radcliffe line: Fraunces labels for Lahore, Amritsar, Delhi, Calcutta in four scripts; a madder line is drawn across the map by the narrator's line 'drawn in five weeks'; the line has a shaky, hand-drawn track and is the only moving item; the plates on either side separate by 24 px at its end. (i) A flat tally of the displaced, a single counter in Fraunces that counts only on narrator words, not as a spectacle, in soot-ground and bone-white type, no red. No kinetic type bursts; no word-by-word; no particles; no glow.

perExhibit.douglass: The Composing Stick. Iron-gall brown-black ground with real letterpress paper tooth under the mount; gold #d9b36a as ink on type, never as foil. Titles in Abril Fatface assembled line by line into a composing stick; plates arrive on a printed mat with a 6-frame squash and then hold. The 1845 Narrative page is held full and still with a gold underline tracing 'Written by Himself'. The faced paintings are retired in favour of silhouette frames; the daguerreotype and the 1845 title page lead. No blur-fill behind plates: the ground is the paper stock. Distressing material is gated by a still plate and a held gate card in the same slab type, never animated. Section changes use the Lock-Up; the rest are Page Lifts.
perExhibit.ford: The Punch Card. Anton in #ff4b1f on iron-grey, stencil and time-clock punch language: a plate slides in like a part on the rail, a parts-bin tag stamps the year, a punch hole animates in the corner at each cut. The line is acted as rhythm: the five-dollar day beat lands on a hard downbeat, the B-24 painting is the single full-bleed moment, labelled. Ford himself is a photograph or turned away, never painted as hero. The Beliefs and Morals section is shot in the same grammar, same type size, same speed, no lamp and no score swell: the real Independent masthead is held 6 s with the narrator, plain cut, and the 1927 retraction stated flat. Involve a Jewish museum partner before it ships.
perExhibit.persia: The Road Line. Midnight ground, lapis #4f7cff, Cormorant Garamond with real Syriac and Chinese script large and faded (6 percent) behind and then lit at reading speed when they are the subject. One line is the whole film: it draws across the screen at each place change and re-appears as the trade road, the carried scroll, the stele's incised column. Plates are brought in on that line. Seal and manuscript plates sit on rag-paper mounts with their captions below, never over. Reconstructions are marked and kept to places and objects, no faces. Motion is slower, with longer holds and wide easing; the camera drifts 1.5 percent at 14 s per image, the slowest of the family.
perExhibit.partition: The Line. Fraunces on soot, madder red #e8553d used only for the drawn line and for years; titles in Urdu, Hindi, Punjabi and English at equal weight, each proofed by a native reader. The film is built on one gesture: a line being drawn, wavering, and tearing. Plates are real photographs only for faces; reconstructions are maps, rooms and trains, no invented faces. The Torn Line is used once at the Radcliffe beat and once at the end of the film; between them, cuts are plain holds. The displacement counter is a single numeral that rises only on narration, with no red and no music bed. Distressing material (violence) is gated with a held gate card; the film itself carries the human-scale images that survive on the record: ordinary luggage, a station, a hand on a rail.

soundTies: Motion is cut to the narrator's breath, not to the music. Transcribe the narration with word timing (the pipeline already has it), mark each caption block's first stressed syllable and the pause after a full stop, and place every plate change on a pause or breath, never mid-clause: the plate arrives about 6 frames before the narrator's first word of that beat (anticipation) and leaves on the last consonant. The one-frame hold on impact (punch, stamp, lock-up) is paired with a foley hit at about 30 percent of the stamp's final level: a die punch for Ford, wood on metal furniture for Douglass, a soft paper turn for Persia, a pencil-on-map for Partition, all recorded or sourced as real sound and placed on the hold frame, not the first frame of the move. Score: a single sustained bed per film, ducked 8 dB under narration with 400 ms attack and 900 ms release, and a score downbeat used no more than twice for a Beat-Cut. The Radcliffe and Beliefs beats are scored with silence for 2 seconds before the narrator; no swell anywhere under distressing material. Reduced-motion variant is an authored cut list (holds and 150 ms fades), not a disabled animation.
productionMethod: Pillow and ffmpeg for the plate pipeline only: true-aspect, ungraded, scan-edge mount, credit line baked into a separate layer; ffmpeg for the final encode, loudnorm, and the concat. Playwright-rendered HTML/CSS/canvas frame by frame at 24 fps and 1920x1080 is the main engine: one timeline JSON per film (plates, caption blocks with narrator timings, transition names, stamp positions) drives a Web Animations API with custom cubic-bezier and spring curves so every move has anticipation and settle; real fonts load from the Plajah DS tokens and per-exhibit font CSS; export PNG frames and encode. Lottie/dotLottie for the repeated gestures (stamp, punch hole, line draw, lock-up bars, caption rule) authored once and re-used, with the weight curves hand-tuned. Canvas or small WebGL shader only for the ink-pull wipe, rubbing-ink edge, torn line and paper tooth, kept off the plate pixels. Fabula is the assembly bench for narration, music, foley and captions timing (the Melos mixer for ducking). Tela supplies the title cards and the maps as vector layers. Magnific only for faceless reconstructions (rooms, roads, objects), never for faces, always stamped; spend credits last and only on re-frames that fail the faceless rule. Pass: contact-sheet review at every beat, 1-frame hold check, and a reduced-motion cut list per film.
risk: Weight and gesture are expensive and easy to overdo: stamps, squash and punch can turn into a cartoon on a solemn subject, especially Douglass and the Beliefs and Partition beats. Mitigation: all violent or moral beats are plain holds with no gesture; the animation vocabulary goes quiet exactly where the material gets heavy, and that contrast is the point. A second risk is time: 24 fps frame-rendering of four 3 to 4 minute films with hand-tuned curves is a lot of render and review hours, and bespoke per-exhibit gestures could drift if the timeline JSON is not shared. Third: stencil, slab and script faces need native proofing (Urdu, Hindi, Punjabi, Syriac, Chinese) before anything ships.

arguesWith.why: KINETIC will want rhythm, speed and a visible beat-driven cut to carry a 3-4 minute film, and will treat holds as dead air. I hold that in a documentary about people who were enslaved, killed or displaced, a plate that settles with weight and then does nothing is the performance; a kinetic type burst on 'ninety-three minutes' is fine, on 'partition' it is a mistake. Timing and spacing are acting, and a frame held one beat too long is a decision. I will give KINETIC the Beat-Cut, twice per film and no more, and the speed of the Ford assembly line, and refuse them anywhere near a distressing plate.
